items.stem: Which of the following historical protests has the strongest continuities with the event shown in the painting?
items.stimulus: The Burning of Jamestown, 1676 “Whereas complaint has been made to this Board by Capt. William Pierce, Esq., that six of his servants and a negro of Mr. Reginald’s has plotted to run away unto the Dutch plantation from their said masters,…the court taking the same into consideration as a dangerous precedent for the future time (if left unpunished), did order that Christopher Miller, a Dutchman (a prime agent in the business), should receive the punishment of whipping,…the said Peter Milcocke to receive thirty stripes and to be Burnt in the cheek with the letter R,…said Richard Cockson, after his full time Expired with his master, to serve the colony for two years and a half, and the said Richard Hill to remain upon his good behavior until the next offense, and the said Andrew Noxe to receive thirty stripes, and the said John Williams, a Dutchman and a [surgeon] after his full time of service is Expired with his master, to serve the colony for seven years, and Emanuel, the Negro, to receive thirty stripes and to be burnt in the cheek with the letter R and to work in shackles one year or more as his master shall see cause.” Source: General Court Responds to Runaway Servants and Slaves Minutes of the Council and General Court of Colonial Virginia, 1640
options: The Whiskey Rebellion
The Montgomery Bus Boycott
Nat Turner’s Rebellion
The Bonus Expeditionary Force March on Washington
items.explanation: Correct: (C). The painting depicts Bacon’s Rebellion (1676), when Nathaniel Bacon’s followers burned Jamestown — a revolt of indentured servants and small farmers against the colonial elite, fueled by the labor grievances described in the court record above. Of the choices, Nat Turner’s Rebellion (1831) is the closest parallel: an uprising of bound laborers against the plantation order, met with brutal retaliation. The Whiskey Rebellion was a tax dispute, the Montgomery Bus Boycott a nonviolent civil-rights protest, and the Bonus Expeditionary March a veterans’ compensation protest — none centered on the revolt of servants and enslaved laborers against their masters.

visual_adaptation.image_caption: Howard Pyle, 'The Burning of Jamestown,' 1905.
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: Pyle's 1905 painting above depicts the burning of Jamestown during Bacon's Rebellion (1676).
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image shows Bacon's rebels burning Jamestown; key C (strongest continuities) is a judgment call unaffected by the image.

items.stem: Why were confrontations such as those in the excerpt rare in the New England colonies?
items.stimulus: The Burning of Jamestown, 1676 “Whereas complaint has been made to this Board by Capt. William Pierce, Esq., that six of his servants and a negro of Mr. Reginald’s has plotted to run away unto the Dutch plantation from their said masters,…the court taking the same into consideration as a dangerous precedent for the future time (if left unpunished), did order that Christopher Miller, a Dutchman (a prime agent in the business), should receive the punishment of whipping,…the said Peter Milcocke to receive thirty stripes and to be Burnt in the cheek with the letter R,…said Richard Cockson, after his full time Expired with his master, to serve the colony for two years and a half, and the said Richard Hill to remain upon his good behavior until the next offense, and the said Andrew Noxe to receive thirty stripes, and the said John Williams, a Dutchman and a [surgeon] after his full time of service is Expired with his master, to serve the colony for seven years, and Emanuel, the Negro, to receive thirty stripes and to be burnt in the cheek with the letter R and to work in shackles one year or more as his master shall see cause.” Source: General Court Responds to Runaway Servants and Slaves Minutes of the Council and General Court of Colonial Virginia, 1640
options: New England populations were largely homogenous with economies based on subsistence farming, rather than cash crops.
Puritan law forbade the sale or ownership of enslaved people.
Indentured servants in New England were largely treated fairly, serving for short terms before gaining freedom.
Negotiations after King Philip’s War had ensured the return of indentured servants back to Europe.
items.explanation: The lives of English settlers in New England and the Chesapeake differed considerably. Entire families tended to emigrate to New England; in the Chesapeake, immigrants were often single males. The climate in New England was more hospitable, and so New Englanders tended to live longer and have larger families than Chesapeake residents. A stronger sense of community, and the absence of tobacco as a cash crop, led New Englanders to settle in larger towns that were closer to one another; those in the Chesapeake lived in smaller, more spread-out farming communities.

visual_adaptation.image_caption: Howard Pyle, 'The Burning of Jamestown,' 1905.
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: Pyle's 1905 painting above depicts the burning of Jamestown during Bacon's Rebellion (1676).
visual_adaptation.key_check: Same image as q01; key A (New England homogeneity/subsistence) is unaffected.

items.stem: The excerpt best supports which one of the following conclusions?
items.stimulus: The Burning of Jamestown, 1676 “Whereas complaint has been made to this Board by Capt. William Pierce, Esq., that six of his servants and a negro of Mr. Reginald’s has plotted to run away unto the Dutch plantation from their said masters,…the court taking the same into consideration as a dangerous precedent for the future time (if left unpunished), did order that Christopher Miller, a Dutchman (a prime agent in the business), should receive the punishment of whipping,…the said Peter Milcocke to receive thirty stripes and to be Burnt in the cheek with the letter R,…said Richard Cockson, after his full time Expired with his master, to serve the colony for two years and a half, and the said Richard Hill to remain upon his good behavior until the next offense, and the said Andrew Noxe to receive thirty stripes, and the said John Williams, a Dutchman and a [surgeon] after his full time of service is Expired with his master, to serve the colony for seven years, and Emanuel, the Negro, to receive thirty stripes and to be burnt in the cheek with the letter R and to work in shackles one year or more as his master shall see cause.” Source: General Court Responds to Runaway Servants and Slaves Minutes of the Council and General Court of Colonial Virginia, 1640
options: English colonists sought to control the native populations through missions and religious conversions.
Trade alliances with Native Americans promoted the economic health of early Chesapeake settlements.
A shortage of indentured servants led to the emergence of the African slave trade.
Chesapeake labor-intensive agriculture used both white and African indentured servants
items.explanation: The excerpt mentions only one of the servants as Negro (Emanuel), so you can logically infer that both white and Black people served in this capacity. Choices (A), (B), and (C) are all unsupported by the excerpt.

items.stem: The first important cash crop in the American colonies was
options: cotton
corn
tea
tobacco
items.explanation: Virginia, one of the earliest colonies, developed around the tobacco trade; tobacco was the colonies’ first important cash crop. Choice (A), cotton, did not become a major export until the early 19th century, when the invention of the cotton gin made large-scale cotton farming practical.

visual_adaptation.image_caption: John Rolfe, who pioneered tobacco cultivation in Virginia (illustration, 1874).
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: The 1874 illustration above shows John Rolfe, who pioneered tobacco cultivation in Virginia.
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image identifies Rolfe with tobacco; key D (tobacco) is directly supported.

items.stem: The pamphlet's denunciation of Quaker officials as 'friends of savages' best reveals which of the following about its authors?
items.stimulus: Frontier settlers at Conestoga and Lancaster (1763–64), furious that the colonial government would not protect them from Native raids yet restrained their retaliation, murdered peaceful Conestoga Indians and then marched on Philadelphia — denouncing Quaker officials as friends of 'savages' and indifferent to frontier suffering. — paraphrased from the Paxton pamphlet literature
options: (A) Their belief that the eastern-dominated government cared more about Indians than about frontier settlers' lives.
(B) Their opposition to any further westward expansion.
(C) Their desire for closer alliance with the British crown.
(D) Their support for Quaker pacifism as a governing philosophy.
items.explanation: The Paxton pamphleteers were furious that the colonial government would neither protect them from Native raids nor let them retaliate — then marched on Philadelphia denouncing Quaker officials as friends of 'savages' indifferent to frontier suffering. The charge exposes their conviction that the eastern elite valued Indian lives over settlers' lives.

visual_adaptation.image_caption: 'The Paxton Boys march on Philadelphia,' 1764.
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: The 1764 print above shows the Paxton Boys' march on Philadelphia described in the passage.
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image shows the 1764 march; key A (eastern government cared more about Indians than settlers) is supported.

items.explanation: The signers, finding themselves outside any existing authority, covenanted to 'combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politick' -- creating a government whose authority came from the mutual agreement of the governed. The Compact did not declare independence (the signers called themselves 'Loyal Subjects'), grant universal suffrage, or invite direct royal rule.
options: A. Direct rule of the colony by the English crown
B. The colony's independence from England
C. Government resting on the consent of the colonists themselves
D. Voting rights for all inhabitants of the colony
items.stem: The phrase 'civil Body Politick' in the Compact is most significant because it established
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"We, whose names are underwritten, the Loyal Subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James... Having undertaken for the Glory of God, and Advancement of the Christian Faith, and the Honour of our King and Country, a Voyage to plant the first Colony in the northern Parts of Virginia; Do by these Presents, solemnly and mutually, in the Presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politick, for our better Ordering and Preservation..."
—Mayflower Compact, 1620 (abridged)

visual_adaptation.image_caption: Robert Weir, 'Embarkation of the Pilgrims,' 1843.
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: Weir's 1843 painting above depicts the Pilgrims' departure — the voyagers who formed the 'civil Body Politick' of the Compact.
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image depicts the Pilgrims' departure; key C (consent of the governed) is unaffected.

items.stem: Which of the following groups would most likely support the principles expressed in the passage above?
items.stimulus: “In the name of God, Amen. We, whose names are underwritten, the loyal subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James, by the Grace of God, of Great Britain, France, and Ireland King, Defender of the Faith, etc. Having undertaken for the Glory of God and advancement of the Christian Faith, and the Honor of our King and Country, a Voyage to plant the First Colony in the Northern Parts of Virginia, do by these presents, solemnly and mutually, in the presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politic, for our better ordering and preservation and furtherance of the ends aforesaid; and by virtue hereof do enact, constitute, and frame such just and equal Laws, Ordinances, Acts, Constitutions and Offices from time to time, as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general good of the Colony, unto which we promise all due submission and obedience. In witness whereof we have hereunder subscribed our names at Cape Cod, the 11th of November, in the year of the reign of our Sovereign Lord King James, of England, France and Ireland the eighteenth, and of Scotland the fifty-fourth. Anno Domini 1620.” Source: William Bradford, Mayflower Compact , 1646
options: A 1600s plantation owner
A Separatist minister
An English Catholic refugee
A representative of the English monarch
items.explanation: Because these settlers were moving to Plymouth, plantation owners were in much smaller supply here compared to the Chesapeake region, so eliminate (A). While the Puritans might have considered themselves refugees, Catholics were generally not welcome in their society, eliminating (C). Puritans generally found themselves on the opposite side of the monarchy in the 1600s, so remove (D). Choice (B) makes the most sense because “Separatists” is another word for Puritan.

visual_adaptation.image_caption: William Halsall, 'Mayflower in Plymouth Harbor,' 1882.
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: Halsall's 1882 painting above shows the Mayflower in Plymouth Harbor — the Separatists' arrival.
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image shows the Pilgrims' arrival; key B (Separatist minister) is unaffected.

B. To grow staple crops such as tobacco
C. To supply raw materials such as lumber
D. Both B and C

items.stem: The Zenger trial is best described as which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"It is … a right, which all free men claim, that they are entitled to complain when they are hurt. … It is not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone … It is the cause of liberty." —Andrew Hamilton, defense of printer John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735 (abridged)

options.text: A colonial dispute over British taxation policy
An early attack on the institution of slavery
A landmark case concerning voting rights
A landmark case concerning freedom of expression

items.explanation: Zenger was tried for seditious libel after printing criticisms of New York's royal governor. Hamilton's acquittal victory established that truthful criticism of officials should not be punished, a milestone for press freedom.

visual_adaptation.image_caption: Andrew Hamilton defending John Peter Zenger in court, 1734-1735 (illustration, 1877-1896).
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: The illustration above shows Andrew Hamilton defending printer John Peter Zenger in court.
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image shows Hamilton's defense; key D (freedom of expression) is directly supported.

items.stem: The speaker above would be most associated with which of the following social or political movements?
items.stimulus: “As for the lawfulness of keeping slaves, I have no doubt, since I hear of some that were bought with Abraham’s money, and some that were born in his house.—And I cannot help thinking, that some of those servants mentioned by the Apostles in their epistles, were or had been slaves. It is plain, that the Gibeonites were doomed to perpetual slavery, and though liberty is a sweet thing to such as are born free, yet to those who never knew the sweets of it, slavery perhaps may not be so irksome.” Source: George Whitefield, 1751
options: Republicanism
Abolitionism
The Age of Reason
The First Great Awakening
items.explanation: If you recognized Whitefield’s name, then this one is a slam dunk. Otherwise, use POE. Choice (B) is the opposite of what you’re looking for. Choices (A) and (C) are unrelated to the topic.

visual_adaptation.image_caption: George Whitefield preaching to a crowd (engraving, 1857).
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: The 1857 engraving above shows the speaker, George Whitefield, preaching to a crowd.
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image identifies the speaker as Whitefield; key D (First Great Awakening) is directly supported.

items.explanation: The French sought furs, not farmland, so they built trading partnerships and alliances with Native peoples rather than displacing them. The Spanish imposed forced labor through the encomienda, while the English seized land for farms, provoking repeated conflict.

B. The Dutch
C. The French
D. The English

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the colony of Pennsylvania?
items.stimulus:
Questions 45–48 refer to the following document.

William Penn's Charter of Privileges, granted to the inhabitants of Pennsylvania and the Territories on October 28, 1701, which guaranteed religious toleration and representative government.

options.text: A charter colony, in which the king granted a charter to colonists
A proprietary colony governed by a proprietor
A royal colony, in which the king appointed the governor
An independent colony operating outside the king's authority

items.explanation: Charles II granted Pennsylvania to William Penn personally, making it a proprietary colony: Penn and his heirs owned and governed it. It was neither a corporate charter colony, a royal colony, nor independent of the crown.

visual_adaptation.image_caption: Thomas Holme's Map of Pennsylvania, 1687.
visual_adaptation.stem_addendum: Holme's 1687 map above shows William Penn's planned colony of Pennsylvania.
visual_adaptation.key_check: Image shows Penn's laid-out colony; key B (proprietary colony) is unaffected.

C. Let New England colonies air common grievances
D. Placed the king in direct control of New England affairs
